vulnerability: Unbound permit and arbitrary from/token allow direct theft of approved underlying tokens
reason: The function accepts arbitrary from and token and calls EIP-2612 permit with spender address(this). The signature only authorizes the router to spend amount of _underlying; it does not bind token or final to. An attacker can observe a valid permit signature and front-run with a malicious token contract whose underlying() returns the victim's token. The router then calls permit on the victim's token and safeTransferFrom(_underlying, from, token, amount), sending the victim's underlying directly to the attacker-controlled token contract. The subsequent depositVault and burn calls are made on the malicious contract and can be no-ops. Even with a legitimate token, the attacker can substitute to=attacker and toChainID to have the burn event credited to the attacker. There is no from==msg.sender check. This is exploitable in the real world via permit front-running and results in direct theft or unauthorized bridge withdrawal.

vulnerability: Unbound permit and arbitrary from/path[0] allow direct theft of approved underlying tokens
reason: The function accepts arbitrary from and path[0], calls EIP-2612 permit with spender address(this), and then transfers _underlying from from to path[0]. The permit signature only authorizes the router to spend amountIn of _underlying; it does not bind path[0] or the final to address. An attacker can front-run a valid permit signature by setting path[0] to a malicious contract whose underlying() returns the victim's token. The router will call permit on the victim's token and safeTransferFrom(_underlying, from, path[0], amountIn), sending the victim's underlying directly to the attacker-controlled path[0] contract. The calls to depositVault and burn on path[0] can be no-ops in the malicious contract. Even if a legitimate anyToken is used, the attacker can set to=attacker and toChainID to have the emitted bridge event credited to the attacker. The ensure(deadline) modifier only checks expiry and does not bind the recipient or path, so this is a real-world permit front-running theft.

reason: This function has the same unsafe permit pattern: it accepts arbitrary from and path[0], calls EIP-2612 permit with spender address(this), and then transfers _underlying from from to path[0]. The signature does not bind path[0] or the final to address, and the function does not require from==msg.sender.
